title: Lock the front door: rulesets and the review rules

story: The platform is two weeks away from the first agent pushing code, and someone asks a simple question in the team channel: when Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, opens a pull request on fcp, what stops that PR from being merged into main by a bot? You open fcp's settings and find the honest answer: almost nothing. There is a ruleset for main, a named set of rules that GitHub enforces on a branch, and it asks for one approval and green tests. Somebody wrote it months ago and then switched it off.

Switching it on looks like one click. But fcp is the repo every engineer works in, and a dozen pull requests are open right now. Click it the wrong way and by lunch every one of them is stuck, waiting for a check that will never arrive. An urgent production fix waits behind a rule nobody remembers agreeing to, and the first message in Slack is "who decided this?"
hook.question: How do you switch on a rule that every change to main must pass, without breaking the honest work that is already in flight?

read.h: People agree first, then the machine enforces
p: A ruleset is a wall: GitHub enforces it for everyone, whatever their token can do, so a fooled agent cannot talk its way past it. That strength is also why it must be agreed before it is switched on. The day the wall blocks someone, they will ask why, and the answer has to be a short page that the engineering leads signed, not an argument in a pull request.

So the first step is a thirty-minute meeting with the two engineering leads, with four rules on the table. Every pull request needs exactly one approval. Any engineer may review any area, so a backend engineer can approve a frontend change and the other way round. The requester never approves their own agent's pull request. And there is no CODEOWNERS file, the GitHub file that forces reviewers by folder, because it would bring back the idea that only some people may review some areas.

Two more answers come out of the same meeting. The first is who the requester is: for Nova, the person who assigned the Jira ticket to it; for a routine, which is Nova started by an event such as a red build, the routine's named owner. Anyone who pushed a commit to the pull request cannot approve it either. The second is the emergency case, called break-glass: who may merge an urgent production fix without the approval and the checks, and how we notice afterwards. Why one approval and not two? Two approvals double the wait on every pull request, and the one approval is already made to count by a separate check that refuses it when it comes from the requester. You will build that check in the next lesson.

read.h: Every honest pull request must be able to pass
p: The rules people agree on are about approvals. The rules that break a repo on its first day are about checks. A required check is a check run that must report success before the pull request can merge, and GitHub finds it by the job's name and nothing else. You met the two traps in the lesson on rulesets: three jobs that are all named Unit Tests cannot be told apart, and a workflow with a paths: filter does not start at all on a pull request that changes nothing in its folders, so its check never reports and the pull request waits forever.

Before you switch anything on, do a dry run: take the rules and replay today's open pull requests against them, asking one question per pull request. Could it ever merge? A pull request that waits for an approval or has a failing test is fine, because a person can fix that. A pull request that waits for a check that can never report is stuck, and only the break-glass team could ever merge it. The output below comes from the dry run in this lesson's lab, on five pull requests that look like a normal fcp morning, with fcp's three CI workflows as they are today.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why GitHub counts a skipped job as passing
p: GitHub's own documentation describes the trap: a workflow skipped by a path filter leaves its required check in a pending state, and the pull request cannot merge. But a job that starts and is then skipped by its own if: condition reports the status skipped, and a required check accepts skipped as passing. That small difference is the whole fix. The work is skipped inside the workflow instead of the workflow being filtered out from outside.

fcp already has the piece that makes this cheap: a check-changes job that looks at the changed files and sets an output per area. The unit-test job reads that output in its if: condition. On a frontend-only pull request the cloud workflow still starts, runs check-changes for a few seconds, skips Cloud Unit Tests, and reports skipped, so the runners spend almost nothing and the required check is satisfied.

read.h: Make the checks requirable, then prove it
p: The fix is two edits per workflow. Give each unit-test job a name that says which part of fcp it tests, Cloud Unit Tests, Client Unit Tests and Frontend Unit Tests, so each required check matches exactly one job. Then remove the paths: filter from the on: block, and let the check-changes job skip the work instead. Here is the frontend workflow after both edits. Run the dry run again and every pull request can pass: some wait for an approval, one has a failing test that its author must fix, and none is stuck.

code.text:
name: "[FRONTEND] - CI"
on:
  pull_request:
jobs:
  check-changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      frontend: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.frontend }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v3
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            frontend:
              - "frontend/**"
              - "common/**"
  unit-tests:
    name: Frontend Unit Tests
    needs: check-changes
    if: needs.check-changes.outputs.frontend == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: make test-frontend

notes.text: No paths: filter any more, so the workflow starts on every pull request and its jobs always report.
dorny/paths-filter turns the changed files into one true or false output per area.
The exact name the ruleset requires, letter for letter.
Skipped when no frontend file changed. A skipped job reports skipped, which a required check accepts.

read.h: Switch it on, then push against it
p: Only now does an org admin switch the ruleset on. fcp's main ruleset already exists, disabled, so one PUT call to GitHub's API replaces it in place with the agreed rules. Read the pull_request block slowly, because each line closes a gap: one approval, an approval is dismissed when a new commit arrives, and whoever pushed last cannot be the approver. The bypass list has one entry, a team of the two leads, and nothing else. The agents' GitHub App is not on it, so a token that can write code still gets the same answer as everyone: one approval and green checks first.

A wall you have not pushed against is a guess, so the last step is to try. Open a test pull request with no approval and check that the merge button stays grey. Open a frontend-only pull request and check that the cloud and client checks show as skipped and that it merges after one approval. Then export the ruleset as JSON and keep it next to the review-rules page: the page says what people agreed, the JSON says exactly what GitHub enforces, and anyone can compare the two.

code.file: run once by an org admin (agents never change rulesets)
code.text:
TEAM_ID=$(gh api orgs/RhinoHealth/teams/fcp-break-glass --jq .id)

gh api -X PUT repos/RhinoHealth/fcp/rulesets/5937570 --input - <<EOF
{
  "name": "main-branch-protection",
  "target": "branch",
  "enforcement": "active",
  "conditions": { "ref_name": { "include": ["refs/heads/main"], "exclude": [] } },
  "bypass_actors": [
    { "actor_type": "Team", "actor_id": ${TEAM_ID}, "bypass_mode": "pull_request" }
  ],
  "rules": [
    { "type": "deletion" },
    { "type": "non_fast_forward" },
    { "type": "pull_request", "parameters": {
        "required_approving_review_count": 1,
        "dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push": true,
        "require_last_push_approval": true,
        "require_code_owner_review": false,
        "required_review_thread_resolution": false,
        "allowed_merge_methods": ["squash"] } },
    { "type": "required_status_checks", "parameters": {
        "strict_required_status_checks_policy": false,
        "required_status_checks": [
          { "context": "Cloud Unit Tests" },
          { "context": "Client Unit Tests" },
          { "context": "Frontend Unit Tests" } ] } }
  ]
}
EOF

notes.text: Rulesets cannot name single people as bypass actors, only teams, roles and apps, so the two leads form a team first.
active switches enforcement on. Today the value is disabled.
bypass_mode pull_request: the leads may merge a pull request without the rules, but they cannot push straight to main.
A new commit cancels the earlier approvals, so the approval always belongs to the code that merges.
The person who pushed the last commit cannot be the one approver.
false: a pull request does not have to be updated with the newest main before it merges. true would re-run every open pull request after each merge.

p: Every wall needs a door for the day production is down and the tests take forty minutes. Without an agreed door, someone with admin rights switches the ruleset off, merges, and forgets to switch it back on, and for a week anyone can push to main. Break-glass is the agreed door: the team of two leads may merge a pull request without the approval or the checks, GitHub records every bypass, and the platform lead reads that list in the weekly review. A door that is logged and read is part of the wall, not a hole in it.

Two checks stay optional for now. The integration test gate and the SDK workflow each wait for a lock on a shared QA environment, so requiring them on every pull request would make the queue far too slow. On GitHub Enterprise plans a ruleset can also be set to evaluate, which records what it would have blocked without blocking; the dry run gives you the same answer for the checks on any plan.

lab.title: Dry-run a ruleset before you switch it on
needs: A terminal on macOS (the sed command uses the macOS form)
lab.goal: Replay five open pull requests against main's ruleset, find the ones that could never merge, and change three CI workflows until every honest pull request can pass.

guess.q: The ruleset requires Cloud Unit Tests, Client Unit Tests and Frontend Unit Tests. cloud-ci.yml only starts when a file under cloud/ changes. A pull request changes one frontend file. What happens to it?

options.text: Cloud Unit Tests is skipped, and the pull request merges after one approval.
options.why: Skipped needs a job that started and then skipped itself. Here the whole workflow never starts, so nothing reports at all.

options.text: It waits forever: Cloud Unit Tests never reports, so the required check never passes.
options.why: A workflow filtered out by paths: never runs, and GitHub keeps the required check pending. Only a bypass could merge it.

options.text: GitHub notices that the cloud folder did not change and drops the requirement.
options.why: GitHub does not know which checks matter for which folders. A required check is required on every pull request.

lab.fix: A week after the switch, a teammate notices the frontend workflow starting on backend pull requests and adds paths: ["frontend/**"] under pull_request: in frontend-ci.yaml, "to save runner minutes". Copy your workflows/frontend-ci.yaml to fix/frontend-ci.yaml, make that same edit there, and run node dryrun.mjs fix. Find which pull requests are now stuck and why, explain why the saving was already there without the filter, and remove it again.
explain: Why is a pull request that waits for an approval fine, while a pull request that waits for a check that never reports is a problem?
Why does a job skipped by its if: condition satisfy a required check, while a workflow filtered out by paths: does not?
Why must the review rules be agreed and written down before the ruleset is switched on, and not after the first blocked pull request?
lab.done: node dryrun.mjs says 0 of 5 PRs could never merge, and node dryrun.mjs fix shows which pull requests a returning paths: filter would trap.

check.q: You are about to switch main's ruleset on. A dry run says three open pull requests could never merge, because Client Unit Tests never reports on them. What do you do?

options.text: Switch it on and tell people to push an empty commit so CI runs again.
options.why: A new commit runs the same workflows with the same filters, so the check still never reports. The pull requests stay stuck.

options.text: Fix the workflows first, so every job always reports or skips itself, and switch on when the dry run shows nothing stuck.
options.why: The ruleset must be passable by every honest pull request before it is enforced. A check that can never report blocks work that did nothing wrong.

options.text: Leave Client Unit Tests out of the required checks for good.
options.why: That makes the pull requests mergeable by dropping the client tests from the wall. The fix is to make the check report, not to stop requiring it.

check.q: Why are the review rules agreed with the engineering leads and written down before the ruleset is switched on?

options.text: GitHub refuses to activate a ruleset until an org owner approves it in the UI.
options.why: GitHub needs no such approval. An org admin can switch a ruleset on with one API call.

options.text: A written page makes the ruleset run faster.
options.why: The page changes nothing about how GitHub checks a merge.

options.text: The ruleset will block real people, and when it does the answer has to be an agreed rule, including the emergency door, not a debate.
options.why: A wall that nobody agreed to is switched off at the first painful block. An agreed page, with break-glass decided in advance, keeps it on.

check.q: Production is down. The fix is ready, but the unit tests take forty minutes and nobody has approved yet. What is the agreed way to merge it?

options.text: One of the two leads in the break-glass team merges the pull request with a bypass, and the bypass is read in the weekly review.
options.why: That is the door built into the wall: a small team, through a pull request, logged and read afterwards.

options.text: An org admin switches the ruleset to disabled, merges, and switches it back on.
options.why: This works once and then gets forgotten. While it is off, anyone, including an agent's token, can push to main.

options.text: Add the agents' GitHub App to the bypass list for an hour, so Nova can merge its own fix.
options.why: Agents never merge. The App is never a bypass actor, not even for an hour.

p: fcp's main ruleset is the existing, disabled main-branch-protection (id 5937570). DevOps applies it with the PUT above as an org admin, after the three CI jobs are renamed and their paths: filters removed in cloud-ci.yml, client-ci.yml and frontend-ci.yaml. The bypass team is fcp-break-glass with Tal and Nir, and Sean reads the bypass list every week. The exported JSON lives next to the review-rules page in fcp docs/ (or the brain once its page format exists), and the rules are announced in #engineering.

Two known gaps from the plan review: require_last_push_approval already stops the last pusher from approving, so G0-09 should say why its 'anyone who pushed' rule is still needed (it covers every pusher, not only the last one). And the integration-test gate and sdk-ci stay optional until the QA-environment locks are faster.

tickets.why: The meeting with Nir and Tal: the four review rules, who the requester is, break-glass, and the one-page write-up.
Rename the unit-test jobs, remove the paths: filters, create fcp-break-glass, apply the ruleset, and prove it with two test PRs.
The agents' GitHub App, checked to be absent from bypass_actors.
The independent-approval check, added to this ruleset's required checks by its exact name (next lesson).

words.plain: A named set of rules GitHub enforces on some branches for everyone, such as one approval and green checks before a merge.
A check, found by its job name, that must report success (or skipped) before a pull request can merge.
Replaying today's open pull requests against the rules before switching them on, to find any that could never merge.
The person who asked an agent for the work: who assigned the ticket to Nova, or the routine's owner. Never the approver.
The agreed emergency door: a small team may merge without the rules, every use is logged and read.
A team, role or app that a ruleset allows to skip its rules. For fcp, only the break-glass team.

review.q: From memory: the four review rules, and the two other things the leads agree in the same meeting.
review.a: Exactly one approval; anyone may review any area; the requester never approves their own agent's PR; no CODEOWNERS. Plus who the requester is (assigner or routine owner, and nobody who pushed) and the break-glass case.

review.q: A teammate wants to add paths: back to a CI workflow to save runner minutes. What do you answer?
review.a: A filtered workflow never reports, so its required check stays pending and PRs outside that folder can never merge. The check-changes job already saves the minutes by skipping the job, and a skipped job satisfies the required check.

review.q: What do you do right after switching a ruleset on, and why?
review.a: Push against it: a PR without approval must not merge, a frontend-only PR must show the other checks skipped and merge after one approval. Then export the ruleset JSON next to the rules page. A wall you have not tested is a guess.

remember: Agree the rules with people, make every honest pull request able to pass them, and only then switch the wall on and push against it.
